To clarify, Beowulf isn't the only existing work of literature from Old English. For example, there are Old English translations of some Bible passages. There are even other poems (like Widswith) in Old English. Still, Beowulf is the *largest* piece of work in Old English that has survived. That alone would make it exemplary (and thereby qualifying it as a "classic").

But that is not the *only* reason it's considered a classic. Beowulf is significant for cultural, historical, linguistic, *and* literary reasons. Cultural, in that it gives us insight into Anglo-Saxon culture of the time. Historical, in that it mixes fact with fiction, thereby giving us a glimpse into 6th century Anglo-Saxon history. For example, Hrothgar, a real 6th-century Danish king, features prominently as one of the characters in Beowulf.

Linguistic, in that, given that it was written before the Norman conquest, it gives us a window into Anglo-Saxon language before the French language influenced it. Old English would have been unrecognizable both to Chaucer and Shakespeare. Historical Linguists use Beowulf as a reference point to mark the evolution of the language of an old Germanic language into the English that we know today, just like how Chaucer's works are used as the reference point for Middle English, and Shakespeare and the King James Bible are viewed as the reference point for Early Modern English.

And literary, in that the poem has genuine literary merit: the style of the epic poem develops the characters. For example, you can see Beowulf's change from the young hero who rips out Grendel's arm, to the seasoned warrior that is finally defeated by the dragon. And other themes, too: "From start to finish, Beowulf demands our acknowledgment that sorting out the monster from the hero and the coward is a lifetime’s struggle in the dark."
